original_title: Enshrouded in Darkness: Lance Oppenheim, Merritt Wever, and Skyler Gisondo on “Primetime”
summary_en: Dive into the unsettling world of Lance Oppenheim's "Primetime," a film that dissects the moral complexities of a "To Catch a Predator"-style show. Starring Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo, the movie blurs the lines between entertainment and exploitation.

en.title: Lance Oppenheim's 'Primetime' Explores the Dark Side of TV Justice
en.summary: Dive into the unsettling world of Lance Oppenheim's "Primetime," a film that dissects the moral complexities of a "To Catch a Predator"-style show. Starring Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo, the movie blurs the lines between entertainment and exploitation.
en.body:
In the unblinking glare of the television studio, where morality is often manufactured for ratings, **Lance Oppenheim**’s new film, **“Primetime,”** plunges into the murky depths of televised vigilantism. The movie centers on the rise of a show eerily reminiscent of **Chris Hansen**’s infamous “To Catch a Predator,” exploring the sensationalist tactics employed to lure and expose alleged child molesters. Oppenheim masterfully uses contrast to amplify the film's chilling effect, juxtaposing the spiritual weight of its subject matter with the earthy reality of its narrative, and oversaturating ordinary scenes with a piercing, almost accusatory light. This visual and thematic tension underscores the film’s exploration of how a nation grapples with sin and vice through the lens of spectacle.

At the heart of **“Primetime”** is the ambitious drive for viewership, embodied by **Robert Pattinson**’s portrayal of the show’s host, a figure who blurs the lines between hunter and hunted, predator and prey. Pattinson's histrionic performance is set against a more understated register from actors like **Merritt Wever**, who plays his producer, Andie, and **Skyler Gisondo**, as Dan Plum, an actor hired as a decoy. Gisondo’s character is tasked with luring out potential predators, a role that frames him as a protégé in Hansen’s morally ambiguous crusade. Hansen, in turn, is depicted as a complex figure, part wolf in sheep’s clothing, part false prophet, who views his show not as a cleansing act but as a vehicle for personal notoriety and power. Oppenheim imbues this narrative with a metaphysical heft, suggesting that Hansen’s actions are framed as a righteous battle against ancient evil, even as the show’s pursuit of higher ratings—with ambitions to be “bigger than 'Lost!'”—ultimately leads to its downfall after a botched exposure.

## The Uncanny Valley of TV Justice

The very concept of a show like the one depicted in **“Primetime”** feels both incredible and disturbingly plausible, a testament to television’s insatiable appetite for drama and confession. Oppenheim’s direction leans into this uncanny valley, where myth and unreality collide. The film doesn't shy away from the ethical quagmire of using deception to extract confessions, highlighting the exploitative nature of such programming. The tension between the perceived righteousness of the mission and the underlying exploitation is palpable, forcing viewers to question the nature of justice when it’s packaged as entertainment. The film’s narrative simplicity is complicated by this deeper exploration of the psychological and moral costs involved, both for the perpetrators and those who orchestrate their downfall.

## What's Next for Oppenheim

While **“Primetime”** marks a significant exploration into the darker corners of media and morality, details regarding its official release date and wider distribution plans have not yet been announced. Fans eager to see **Lance Oppenheim**’s distinctive vision brought to life, particularly in its examination of sensationalism and the pursuit of fame, will want to stay tuned for further updates on this compelling and provocative film.

content_raw: Blurring–or rather smudging–the lines between hunter and hunted, predator and prey, exploiter and exploited, director Lance Oppenheim’s “ Primetime ” derives its deliciously devilish thrills through emphasizing contrast. Whether it is imbuing spiritual weight to the earthiness of its story, oversaturating its ordinary compositions with piercing, revealing light, or contrasting a histrionic performance from an unhinged Robert Pattinson –who plays “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen–against an actor in a more understated register, the film exists in that uncanny valley between myth and unreality. Even the very concept of Hansen’s show, wherein he and his team would draw potential child molesters out, where he would then confront them and force them to confess to their twisted desires, feels incredulous that it was ever on air, and also par for the course for a nation that regularly resorts to spectacle and entertainment when it comes to trying to process sin and vice. Straightforward as it may be in telling its story about the rise of Hansen’s show, the boundaries he pushed in the pursuit of higher ratings (“I’m gonna be bigger than “Lost!” he ambitiously exclaims to his producer, Andie [ Merritt Wever ]), and the show’s subsequent cancellation after an exposure gone wrong, its simplicity is complicated through how Oppenheim imbues a metaphysical heft into its narrative. “You’re cleansing the world of an ancient evil,” Hansen tells his protégé, Dan Plum ( Skyler Gisondo ), an actor hired as a decoy to lure out the potential predators. Indeed, Hansen exists somewhere between a wolf in sheep’s clothing and a false prophet, framing his show as righteous when, in reality, he sees it as a way to gain more notoriety and power. For Oppenheim, this tension is something he was excited to explore in his first feature film, after a string of successful documentaries. “There’s something so interesting and maybe somewhat tragic about the concept of a person who has essentially embraced the cultural lore around himself,” he shared. With “Primetime” breaking out at the box office, introducing Hansen to a whole new host of viewers, Oppenheim, Wever, and Gisondo spoke with RogerEbert.com over Zoom before the film’s premiere in New York; this piece combines their interviews into one fluid conversation. They discussed the film’s unique spiritual temperament, chewing gum, child actors, and whether it is ever possible to truly offer help on the other side of a camera. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. Merritt, one piece of audio that “Primetime” highlights is your voracious gum chewing. Tell me more about how that action helped you, if at all, understand Andie better? Merritt Wever: I went through a hundred packs of whatever was sugar-free, but I definitely chewed so much that by the end of the day I was getting nauseous.
